title: Question 5
stem:
Fig. 5.1 shows four diodes and a load resistor of resistance $1.2\text{k}\Omega$, connected in a circuit that is used to produce rectification of an alternating voltage.
{{figure:figure_5_1}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by rectification.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what kind of current your phone charger takes from the mains and what kind it must supply to the battery - what change has to happen?
parts.proper_answer: Rectification is the conversion of alternating current (a.c.) to direct current (d.c.).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a.c. and d.c. mean**
Think of a.c. as current that keeps reversing direction, and d.c. as current in one direction only. Most electronic devices need d.c. but the mains supplies a.c.

Step 2: **Define rectification**
So rectification is simply the process of turning that reversing a.c. into a unidirectional d.c., using diodes that allow current in one direction only.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State the type of rectification produced by the circuit in Fig. 5.1.
hints: Hint 1: Count the diodes in Fig. 5.1 and recall what a diamond of four diodes does to both halves of the a.c. cycle.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the bridge**
You have four diodes arranged in a diamond. That is the classic bridge rectifier. A single diode would only keep one half of the cycle.

Step 2: **Full versus half**
With four diodes the circuit steers current the same way through the load on both positive and negative halves of the input, so both halves are used. That is called full-wave rectification.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: A sinusoidal alternating voltage $V_{\text{IN}}$ is applied across the input terminals X and Y. The variation with time $t$ of $V_{\text{IN}}$ is given by the equation $$V_{\text{IN}} = 6.0 \sin 25\pi t$$ where $V_{\text{IN}}$ is in volts and $t$ is in seconds.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.1, label the output terminals P and Q with the appropriate symbols to indicate the polarity of the output voltage $V_{\text{OUT}}$.
hints: Hint 1: Follow the diode arrow symbols in Fig. 5.1 - current can only flow in the direction of the arrow, so which output lead must always be pushed positive?
parts.proper_answer: P is positive (+) and Q is negative (-), so current always flows from P through the load to Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Follow the arrows**
A diode conducts only in the direction of its triangle arrow. Trace either half-cycle of $V_{IN}$ through the bridge and you will find current is always directed to flow into one side of the resistor and out of the other.

Step 2: **Fix the polarity**
In this layout the top lead to the resistor is always at higher potential. So label P with $+$ and Q with $-$. The polarity of $V_{OUT}$ never reverses, even though $V_{IN}$ does.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: VOUT scale labelled 4 and 8 on the 2 cm tick marks
t scale labelled 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12 on the 2 cm tick marks

hints: Hint 1: Look at the form $V_{IN} = V_0 \sin \omega t$ - what tells you the peak value and what tells you how fast it oscillates?
Hint 2: Recall $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi / T$ for the input, then think carefully about how the period of the rectified output compares to the input period.
Hint 3: Use the peak to set the $V_{OUT}$ scale and the new period to set the $t$ scale on Fig. 5.2 with its regular grid.
parts.proper_answer: Peak $V_{OUT} = 6.0\text{ V}$. Input period $T_{IN} = 2\pi/25\pi = 0.080\text{ s}$, so rectified period $T_{OUT} = 0.040\text{ s}$. $V_{OUT}$ axis: 0, 4.0, 8.0 V on 2 cm marks. $t$ axis: 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12 s on 2 cm marks.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the peak from the equation**
Compare $$V_{IN} = 6.0 \sin 25\pi t$$ with $$V = V_0 \sin \omega t$$ You can read straight off $V_0 = 6.0\text{ V}$ and $\omega = 25\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. Ideal diodes drop no voltage, so the peak of $|V_{OUT}|$ is also $6.0\text{ V}$. That fixes the vertical scale, for example 4.0 V and 8.0 V on the heavy 2 cm grid lines.

Step 2: **Find the input period**
Angular frequency links to period by $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ so $$T_{IN} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{25\pi} = 0.080\text{ s}$$ That is the time for one full sine wave of input.

Step 3: **Halve the period for full-wave**
Full-wave rectification flips the negative half up, so you get two output humps per input cycle. Hence $$T_{OUT} = \frac{T_{IN}}{2} = 0.040\text{ s}$$ On Fig. 5.2 the zeros occur every 0.040 s. Labelling the heavy 2 cm divisions as 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12 s fits three humps exactly.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: The output voltage in (b) is smoothed by adding a capacitor to the circuit in Fig. 5.1. The difference between the maximum and minimum values of the smoothed output voltage is 10% of the peak voltage.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.1, draw the circuit symbol for a capacitor showing the capacitor correctly connected into the circuit.

markscheme_points.text: correct symbol used for capacitor and capacitor connected in parallel with the 1.2

hints: Hint 1: For smoothing you want the capacitor to charge up to the peak and then supply current to the load when the rectified voltage falls - across which component must it be connected to do this?
parts.proper_answer: Connect a capacitor in parallel with the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ load resistor, between P and Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Act as a reservoir**
Smoothing works because the capacitor stores charge at the peak and releases it to the resistor when the supply dips. To do that it must see the same voltage as the load.

Step 2: **Parallel connection**
So draw the standard two-parallel-line capacitor symbol directly across the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor, one plate to P and one plate to Q.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.2, sketch the variation with $t$ of the smoothed output voltage.

markscheme_points.text: straight lines or curves, with negative decreasing gradients, drawn between adjacent line going up to next peak
lines, from one peak to the line going up to the next peak, show a drop in p.d. of

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens after a peak - the capacitor discharges slowly through the resistor instead of the voltage falling straight to zero.
Hint 2: The ripple is given as 10% of the 6.0 V peak, so how far below each peak should your curve fall before the next rise meets it?
parts.proper_answer: Slightly drooping, almost straight lines joining each 6.0 V peak to a point 0.60 V lower on the rising edge of the next unsmoothed hump, never reaching zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shape of the smoothed trace**
Between peaks the capacitor discharges through the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor. The discharge is exponential, but over a short time it looks like a straight line with a small negative gradient. Start each section at the 6.0 V peak.

Step 2: **Size of the ripple**
Ripple $= 10\%$ of peak $= 0.10 \times 6.0 = 0.60\text{ V}$. So each line falls only to about $5.4\text{ V}$ before it meets the sharply rising next hump, then rises quickly back to the next peak. The curve stays near the top and never goes to zero.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance $C$ of the capacitor.
hints: Hint 1: Work out the lowest voltage of the ripple from 10% of the 6.0 V peak - this is the voltage left after discharge.
Hint 2: Recall the discharge equation linking voltage, time, resistance and capacitance, and identify the discharge time for one ripple cycle.
Hint 3: Rearrange $V = V_0 \exp(-t/RC)$ to solve for $C$, checking that $R$ is in ohms and $t$ in seconds.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the discharge voltages and time**
Peak $V_0 = 6.0\text{ V}$. Ripple $= 0.10 \times 6.0 = 0.60\text{ V}$, so minimum $$V = 6.0 - 0.60 = 5.4\text{ V}$$ The capacitor discharges from 6.0 V to 5.4 V in almost one output period. Allowing for the short charging time, discharge time $t \approx 0.034\text{ s}$ from the graph.

Step 2: **Apply exponential discharge**
Discharge follows $$V = V_0 \exp\left(\frac{-t}{RC}\right)$$ with $R = 1.2\text{ k}\Omega = 1.2 \times 10^3\, \Omega$. Substitute: $$5.4 = 6.0 \exp\left[\frac{-0.034}{(1.2 \times 10^3) C}\right]$$

Step 3: **Solve for C**
Divide by 6.0: $$0.90 = \exp\left[\frac{-0.034}{(1.2 \times 10^3) C}\right]$$ Take natural logs: $$\ln 0.90 = \frac{-0.034}{(1.2 \times 10^3) C}$$ $$C = \frac{-0.034}{(1.2 \times 10^3)\ln 0.90} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$$ This is about $270\, \mu\text{F}$, a sensible smoothing value.
